title: Family purity
hook: many observant couples keep laws of separation and immersion; it is a private practice

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mikveh: gathered rain and spring water, and Rabbi Akiva's play on the hope of Israel. Your line was living waters. Did water mark a before and after for you? Day one thousand ninety.

Some practices are meant to be seen: a sukkah in the yard, a menorah in the window. This one is meant not to be. A married woman, after a stretch of days apart from her husband, goes down the steps of a mikveh, under the water, and back up. Then the two of them come back together. Her neighbors don't need to know she went. This is what Jewish law calls family purity. Couples who keep it keep it quietly. Today: a practice whose privacy is part of its shape.
screen: `A SUKKAH IN THE YARD.` → `A MENORAH IN THE WINDOW.` → `THIS ONE, UNSEEN.`

segments.voice: Family purity. In Hebrew, taharat hamishpacha. First, the source. Leviticus describes a woman's monthly flow as a time of ritual impurity, and says a husband and wife don't come together during it. The Mishnah gives these laws a whole tractate, Niddah, inside the order of purities you met two days ago. Second, the rhythm. Couples who keep these laws step back from physical closeness during the woman's period and for a time of counting afterward that the rabbis set. Then she immerses in a mikveh, and they come together again. Apart, then together, month after month. Third, a reason. The Talmud asks why the Torah set this up, and Rabbi Meir answers: so that she will be as dear to her husband as on the day she stood under the wedding canopy. That's one voice. Some who keep these laws say they keep them first because they are commanded, and find their meaning from inside the practice. Fourth, what it isn't. Remember the line from two days ago: a state, not a grade. Ritual impurity here says nothing about a woman being dirty or less. It's a status tied to the body's own rhythm, and it ends with water and time. Jews hold these laws in different ways. Orthodox communities teach them as binding law. Some in other movements keep them in adapted forms, and some don't keep them. Across all of that, one thing is shared by those who do: it belongs to the couple. Mikveh visits are kept discreet. Nobody is expected to explain.
screen: `LEVITICUS, AND THE TRACTATE NIDDAH.` · `APART, THEN TOGETHER.` · `AS DEAR AS ON THE WEDDING DAY.` · `A STATE, NOT A GRADE.` · then, large: `A PRIVATE PRACTICE.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: respect one private practice. Sit, and let the breath slow. Think of someone you know who keeps something you don't fully see. A fast. A prayer at a set hour. A food they won't eat. An evening they're never free. Notice any urge to ask about it, to explain it, or to have an opinion. You don't need to act on it. Let their practice stay theirs, whole, without your commentary. Then ask: is there something you keep quietly too? The bell holds the time.
Family purity. Taharat hamishpacha: laws of separation and immersion that observant couples keep, and keep privately. Today's word.
Your line: a private practice. Today, when you notice someone's quiet observance, let it be, without asking them to explain. Day one thousand ninety.

howItsDone: Orthodox couples keep the laws of family purity as binding, with the wife immersing in a mikveh before they resume intimacy; some Jews in other movements keep adapted forms, others do not, and mikveh visits are kept discreet.

original.note: Hebrew: purity of the family, the name for these laws of separation and immersion.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old rule that treats women as unclean.
what it means: a private rhythm of separation and reunion, kept by couples who follow it and marked by immersion in a mikveh.
what a scholar hears: Leviticus 15 and 18:19, the tractate Niddah in the order of purities, and Rabbi Meir's reason in Niddah 31b.

Sensitive day: written to stay general and respectful, with no physical detail beyond separation and immersion. Please review tone carefully.

The index hook says 'many observant couples'; the script avoids 'many' (claims rule) and says 'kept by observant couples'. The teach says some keep them first because they are commanded; please confirm.
The hook's sukkah and menorah are general examples of visible practice, not from the cited texts.
'A time of counting afterward that the rabbis set' deliberately gives no number (the seven clean days); please confirm the description.
Rabbi Meir's reason, Niddah 31b, is paraphrased; please confirm.
The description of how movements differ (Orthodox: binding; some in other movements: adapted; some: not kept) is meant to be neutral and unranked; please confirm.
The term 'taharat hamishpacha' is a later name for these laws rather than a Mishnaic one; the script does not claim otherwise.
